title: Family retraces last steps
subtitle: One month after Byron Debassige was gunned down by police in a Davisville-area park, his family and friends returned to the scene to retrace his final steps.
article: One month after Byron Debassige was gunned down by police in a Davisville-area park, his family and friends returned to the scene to retrace his final steps.
"I first want to return the lemon my brother stole," Angie Assinewe told a clerk at D&Y Market on Yonge St., handing over a fruit she brought from home.
It was here that the string of events leading up to Debassige's death began.
Debassige, who suffered from mental illness, had stolen some lemons from the convenience store around 8:15 p.m. on Feb. 16.
A clerk chased him out of the store, but the 28-year-old pulled out a small knife. He then took off across Yonge St. and headed west on Chaplin Cres.
This is where Assinewe and about 20 others marched next. Many carried the yellow fruit in protest.
"He was homeless, but he always had a home. I miss him. I miss him so much," said Ken Assinewe, Debassige's father.
Debassige's mother, Jennifene, who lives on Manitoulin Island, wanted to come, but has become ill due to stress and is in the hospital, Assinewe said.
Several women in the crowd had worked with Debassige at the Aboriginal Legal Services of Toronto. The group has called for an inquest into the shooting.
"We need to make sure this doesn't happen again," said Kimberly Murray, the executive director.
"It is quite clear to me that (police) could use some more training dealing with the mentally ill. Maybe they've started on the right path, but more needs to be done," she said.
Murray said they are eagerly awaiting the results of an investigation by the Special Investigations Unit, a civilian agency that probes cases of serious injury or death involving police.
Debassige struggled with drugs and alcohol use and has spent time in jail, but he was not violent, his family said.
Assinewe said the family is worried the SIU won't be able to get past his darker side and will exonerate the police.
Toronto police are not allowed to comment on that night because the SIU is investigating.
A witness heard an officer yell, "Put down the knife! Put down the knife!" before four gunshots echoed across Oriole Park.

Debassige was struck in the chest, although the exact number of times has not been released. "Why didn't the police call for backup?" asked Colette McCombs, 34, who met Debassige through the community. "He was very open. Kind. He loved music."
Beating a small drum, McCombs and several others sang a native honour song in his memory.
"This is the last place where Byron took a breath," said Assinewe, placing a bouquet of daisies in the snow to mark the spot.
Then one by one, the group encircled the flowers with lemons.
